title: The crown (Mark 15:1–20)
hook: Barabbas released, the purple cloak, the crown of thorns

segments.voice: Yesterday, before the cock crows twice: Jesus silent before the council, Peter by the fire. Your line was peter wept. Did you start an apology? Now it's morning, and Jesus is handed to Rome. Day two hundred twenty-nine.

Early in the morning, the chief priests, the elders and the scribes hold a council, bind Jesus, and hand him over to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. Only Rome can crucify. Pilate has a custom at the feast: he releases one prisoner, whoever the crowd asks for. In his jail right now is a man named Barabbas, locked up with rebels who committed murder in an uprising. So Pilate offers the crowd a choice. Jesus, or Barabbas. And a few hours later, soldiers will put a crown on Jesus's head. Not gold.
screen: `HANDED OVER TO PILATE.` → `JESUS, OR BARABBAS?` → `A CROWN, NOT OF GOLD.`

segments.voice: First, Pilate's question. He asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "Art thou the king of the Jews?" And Jesus answers: "Thou sayest it." Then he's silent again, while the chief priests accuse him of many things, and Pilate marvels. Second, the choice. Pilate seems to see that the charge comes out of envy. But the chief priests stir up the crowd to ask for Barabbas. What shall I do with this king, then? Crucify him. And Pilate, wanting to satisfy the crowd, releases Barabbas, has Jesus scourged, and hands him over to be crucified. Here's a detail many readers notice: Barabbas means son of the father, bar abba, in Aramaic. Last night Jesus called God Abba. This morning one son of the father walks free, and the other takes his place. Third, the crown. Roman soldiers lead him into the governor's palace and call together the whole cohort. "And they clothe him with purple, and platting a crown of thorns, they put it upon him. And they began to salute him: Hail, king of the Jews." Purple was the color of emperors. They hit his head with a reed, spit on him, and kneel in mock worship. Fourth, the irony. Every piece of the mockery is true, in Mark's telling. They mean it as a joke: a purple cloak, a crown, a salute, kneeling soldiers. Mark's readers know he really is the king. The soldiers are acting out a coronation without knowing it. Catholics remember this scene in the rosary, the third Sorrowful Mystery, the crowning with thorns. It was Rome's soldiers who mocked him, and Rome that crucified him.
screen: `ART THOU THE KING? THOU SAYEST IT.` · `BARABBAS: SON OF THE FATHER.` · `PURPLE, THORNS, HAIL, KING.` · `A CORONATION THEY DON'T UNDERSTAND.` · then, large: `AND PLATTING A CROWN OF THORNS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for prisoners, or hold them in mind. Settle and breathe. Jesus was a prisoner that morning: bound, mocked, beaten, with no one to speak for him. Right now, millions of people are in prison, some guilty, some not, some forgotten by everyone. Think of one, if you know one. If you don't, picture a cell, and someone sitting in it this morning. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for the people who guard them. If you don't, simply hold them in your attention for a minute. The bell holds the time.
The crown. The crown of thorns Roman soldiers pressed on Jesus's head as a joke, while they hailed him as king. Today's word.
Your line: they mocked the king. Today, when you hear someone being mocked, in person or online, don't join in, and if you can, quietly take their side. Day two hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics meditate on the crowning with thorns as the third Sorrowful Mystery of the rosary, and visiting the imprisoned is one of the Church's corporal works of mercy, carried out through prison ministries in many dioceses.

fork.setup: you're Pilate. the crowd shouts for Barabbas, a rebel. you suspect the charge against Jesus is envy. what do you do?
options: release Barabbas to satisfy the crowd.
fork.reveal: wanting to satisfy the crowd, Pilate releases Barabbas, has Jesus scourged, and hands him over to be crucified.

original.note: Greek: a crown of thorns. stephanos, crown, gives us the name Stephen.

trapdoor: what you thought: soldiers being cruel.
what it means: a mock coronation, purple, crown, salute, kneeling, of the one Mark says really is king.
what a scholar hears: stephanos akanthinos; Barabbas, bar abba, set beside Gethsemane's Abba; purple as imperial color in Roman mockery.

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 15:2 and 15:17–18 given from memory; confirm wording.
Barabbas = bar abba, 'son of the father': a common etymology; confirm. The link to Gethsemane's Abba is presented as what 'many readers notice'.
The crowd and chief priests are named as Mark names them; the script stresses that Rome crucified. Keeper should confirm the balance and tone on this sensitive passage.
Rosary Sorrowful Mysteries and corporal works of mercy (CCC 2447) in howItsDone: confirm.
